analysis.one_liner: Triples the lobbying ban for former members of Congress from two to five years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress before it expired.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already bars former members of Congress from lobbying their old colleagues for a period after leaving office. This bill would have stretched that ban to five years for ex-members, and extended the shorter ban for former congressional staff and officers from one year to two. Violating it would be a federal crime. It would not touch sitting members, their staff salaries, or lobbying by anyone who has never served in Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want former lawmakers to have less influence over the people they just served alongside, and the public's interest in decisions made on the merits rather than on personal connections. It also indirectly protects current members from being lobbied by their recent colleagues.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Citizens who want less insider lobbying

how_it_helps.text: Extends the lobbying ban for former members of Congress from two years to five, so a departing senator or representative cannot sell access to former colleagues for an additional three years [S3].
Lengthens the ban on lobbying contacts by former congressional employees and elected chamber officers from one year to two [S2][S3].
Makes violations a federal crime punishable under the same criminal provisions that apply to other post-employment lobbying violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, who lose three extra years of the lucrative lobbying career that many currently pursue, and lobbying firms that hire them for their connections to sitting lawmakers.

drawbacks.text: The ban applies criminal penalties to lobbying communications, and critics of such bans argue they restrict speech and push influence-seeking into harder-to-trace channels rather than ending it [S3].

It does not address the core of the revolving-door problem while someone is still in office: sitting members can still negotiate future lobbying employment, and the bill only restricts activity after departure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A longer waiting period is a modest, low-cost step against the practice of former lawmakers cashing in on their contacts. It leaves the larger mechanics of influence — campaign donations, K Street hiring negotiations, and lobbying by people who never held office — untouched, so it should be judged a partial fix rather than a solution.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee sent it to its crime subcommittee three weeks later, and no further action ever came before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bill Posey introduced the bill on January 13, 2015 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
On February 5, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations, which is where its progress stopped [S5].
The bill's only cosponsor was a single House Democrat, so its support never grew beyond two members [S4].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action appears in the bill's action history before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying firms that hire them, who face no extended waiting period and can move straight from office into lobbying careers exactly as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Former lawmakers and their lobbying employers

for.name: Rep. Bill Posey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill extending post-employment lobbying bans.

for.name: 1 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making its support bipartisan but minimal.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Bob Goodlatte (R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its crime subcommittee on February 5, 2015 and never scheduled it for a markup or floor consideration in the two years that followed.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Majority leadership controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote at any point in the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: With one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, the bill drew too little support from either party to register a partisan pattern, and it never reached a vote where one could be measured.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and K Street influence shops
industries.note: The bill's five-year ban would shrink the pool of recently departed lawmakers available to lobby, the chief commodity these firms sell. Their business model profits from selling access that ordinary people cannot buy.
Ex-lawmakers would wait five years instead of two before lobbying their former colleagues, delaying the lucrative second career many now take. They are the direct subject of the restriction.
